nodes.description: Biallelic loss-of-function GBA2 variants abolish or drastically reduce the activity of non-lysosomal glucosylceramidase beta 2, an ER/Golgi membrane enzyme that hydrolyzes glucosylceramide to ceramide and glucose. Missense variants in the catalytic domain and truncating variants both yield nonfunctional enzyme; no residual GBA2 glucocerebrosidase activity is detectable in blood cells of homozygous patients.

Gba2-null mice accumulate glucosylceramide in brain, testis, and liver and show globozoospermia and impaired male fertility, establishing GBA2 as a glucosylceramidase whose loss causes a non-lysosomal (ER) glucolipid storage disease. The model recapitulates the storage and male-infertility arms; overt neurological signs were not observed, a translational limitation.

With GBA2 activity lost, glucosylceramide accumulates at the cytosolic face of the ER and Golgi and outside the lysosome, and the broader glycosphingolipid profile is perturbed. In GBA2-deficient mice, glucosylceramide accumulates in brain, testis, and liver; in patients, reduced GBA2 activity raises glucosylceramide to levels comparable with Gaucher disease, defining a non-lysosomal glucosylceramide storage state.

nodes.description: Disturbed glycosphingolipid composition alters membrane microdomain organization and cytoskeletal dynamics. In Gba2-null mice, non-lysosomal glucosylceramide accumulation disrupts microtubule and F-actin organization during spermiogenesis (globozoospermia); by inference the same membrane and cytoskeletal perturbation impairs axonal growth in neurons. In a zebrafish model, gba2 knockdown causes axonal shortening and aberrant branching of motoneurons, rescued by wild-type but not mutant human GBA2.
